This green stripe is caused by a virus-like, parasitic mycoplasma. The result of the infection produces a green or pink stripe on the white petals (https://www.fs.fed.us/.../pla.../trillium_grandiflorum.shtml). Mycoplasma infected trilliums are not uncommon, although I confess, I have seen only a hand-full of populations showing this infection. On that day, this was the only plant I noticed with the green stripe.

description:
a. Life stage
Flowering

b. Origin
Native to Eastern North America

c. Defining traits
- Single, large, 3-petaled white flower (that turns pink with age) on single stalk
- White petals are broad elliptical-shaped with pointed tips
- 3 green sepals under white flower 
- Single whorl of broad, pointed ovate sessile leaves with wavey margins 
- Around 1ft tall 

d. Plant Community
Understory of deciduous forest 

e. Background or Other Interesting Info
- The Legislative Assembly of Ontario adopted the White Trillium as Ontario's official flower in 1937
- The trillium has been the official emblem of Ontario since 1964
- Trillium seeds are mainly dispersed by ants, due to their attraction to the elaiosome on the seeds of trilliums
- White-tailed deer also love to eat the white trillium
- Trilliums are very slow-growing, can take a trillium plant up to 10 years to produce its first flower
- After the first bloom, a trillium will live another 10 to 13 years — but only if it is not damaged

Sources: 
- Dickinson, Richard, and Royer, France. Plants of Southern Ontario. Lone Pine, 2021.

description:
These were the first Trilliums I got to see this Spring, draped in Maple Tree blossoms. I don't know how long they had been blooming, but this is a good place to see some from the road - but not really up close, as this would be private property, and they are across the stream that is carving this pretty ravine. They are scattered on a slope that parallels the small road though. A fine place to drive slowly with binoculars as there is little traffic to contend with. 

These are among my Mother's favorite flowers, so this is a great place to visit this time of year. The Trilliums continue in patches for much of this stretch of road downstream of here. They were all of the White variety as far as I noticed. Trilliums seem to favor shady steep woodland slopes, and so are sometimes relatively inaccessible to those people with limited mobility. I'm always on the lookout for nice areas to visit by car for woodland flower displays such as this.

description:
LIFE STAGE (at the time of observation): Flower Stage (herbaceous perennial forb)
ORIGIN: Native to Ontario
DEFINING TRAITS: Forb with leaves whorled of three atop stem¹, along with three petals (white)/sepals (green). Solitary inflorescence, yellow anthers and pistils.
PLANT COMMUNITY: Shady mixed Forest (Rouge Hill Urban National Park, Scarborough ON)

BACKGROUND OR OTHER INTERESTING INFO: 

This particular trillium observed has been infected with parasitic "mycoplasma organisms, which cause the green striping pattern found in petals of infected"³. This trillium has duplicated an extra whorl of sepals (with two resembling petals) which shows the mycoplasma organism causing green striping.

There are three main uses for the trillium across literature in the Haudenosaunee and Anishinaabe first nations: The first as a root tea for treating and balancing women's reproductive health; the second is a root poultice for tumors, boils or abscesses; and the third is an expectorant tea to treat coughs and similarly, as an astringent for diarrhea or dysentery².

SOURCE:
1. DICKINSON, R. (2021). "Plants of Southern Ontario". LONE PINE MEDIA. 
2. https://gibsurvey.ca/species/red-trillium-white-trillium
3. https://mnfi.anr.msu.edu/abstracts/botany/trillium_undulatum.pdf

description:
**Life stage:** Flowering (perennial)
**Origin:** Native to Ontario
**Defining traits:** 
3 whorled leaves, basal, sessile
Solitary inflorescence:
- 3 white petals (can be tinged pink)
- Visible veins
- Wavy edges
- 3 sepals, offset between petals
- 6 stamens, yellow anthers
- 6-sided ovary

Odourless
Leaves (actually bracts) have net venation (3-7 main parallel veins + smaller connecting veins) even though trillium is a monocot
**Plant community:** Shaded, upland, mixed hardwood forest
**Background info:**
Slow-growing; requires 7-10 years to reach maturity
Seeds are primarily dispersed by ants (myrmecochory) 1 
Preferred food of white-tailed deer 1 
Susceptible to phytoplasma (bacterial parasite) infections which causes extra petals and green-streaked petals 2 
Haudenosaunee and Anishinaabe uses of trillium: 3
- Root tea for treating and balancing women’s reproductive health
- Astringent for diarrhea or dysentery
- Hormone regulator for night sweats
- Expectorant tea to treat coughs

**Sources:**
1. https://blog.ontarioparks.ca/trilliums/
2. https://nargs.org/sites/default/files/free-rgq-downloads/VOL_52_NO_1.pdf

Life Stage:
The White Trillium is in it’s flowering stage in mid-May.

Origin:
The Trillium is native to North America and Asia.

Defining Traits: 
The flowers are whorled with 3 white petals and 2 sepals. The leaves are grouped in three in a whorl position and opposite.

Plant Community:
Found in Central Ganaraska Forest Conservation is the headwaters of the Ganaraska River to protect this vital watershed. 

Other Interesting Facts:
Trillium seeds are primarily spread by ants. It became an Ontario’s flower in 1937. It is a perennial and loves the shade of a forested understory. It is not illegal to pick the plant, but it will not succeed next year when this disturbance of picking takes place.
